'''''Fagopyrum cymosum''''', also known as '''perennial buckwheat'''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tahir |first1=I. |last2=Farooq |first2=S. |title=Grain and Leaf Characteristics of Perennial Buckwheat (Fagopyrum cymosum Meissn.) |journal=Fagopyrum |volume=9 |year=1989 |pages=41–43|url=https://fagopyrum.net/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Fagopyrum cymosum (FAGCY) |url=https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/FAGCY |website=EPPO Global Database |publisher=European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization |access-date=2026-08-13}}</ref> or ''tall buckwheat''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | ''Fagopyrum cymosum'' | 448824 | accessdate=16 December 2014}}</ref> is a [[domestication|domesticated]] [[plant]] used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]],<ref name=FOC>{{cite book |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242100052 |title=Flora of China |author=Li Anjen and Suk-pyo Hong |volume=5 |chapter=''Fagopyrum'' |year=2004}}</ref> for animal feed, and as an ornamental plant.<ref name=GRIN/> It is native to much of China, and to Bhutan, Nepal, India, Burma, and Vietnam.<ref name=FOC/>

==Chemistry==
The flowers are known for their high content of [[fagopyrin]], a naphthodianthrone that provokes phototoxic effects known as fagopyrism.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Stojilkovski | first1 = K. | last2 = Glavač | first2 = N. | last3 = Kreft | first3 = S. | last4 = Kreft | first4 = I. | year = 2013 | title = Fagopyrin and flavonoid contents in common, Tartary, and cymosum Buckwheat | journal = Journal of Food Composition and Analysis | volume = 32 | issue = 2| pages = 126–130 | doi=10.1016/j.jfca.2013.07.005}}</ref>
